definition: In computer vision and image processing, Otsu's method, named after Nobuyuki Otsu (大津展之, Ōtsu Nobuyuki), is used to perform automatic image thresholding.
details: In the simplest form, the algorithm returns a single intensity threshold that separate pixels into two classes – foreground and background. This threshold is determined by minimizing intra-class intensity variance, or equivalently, by maximizing inter-class variance. Otsu's method is a one-dimensional discrete analogue of Fisher's discriminant analysis, is related to Jenks optimization method, and is equivalent to a globally optimal k-means performed on the intensity histogram. The extension to multi-level thresholding was described in the original paper, and computationally efficient implementations have since been proposed.

explainer.lead: Otsu's method picks a single intensity threshold that splits an image into foreground and background without human tuning. That makes it a cheap, automatic first step for many segmentation pipelines.

tiers.eli5: Imagine sorting a pile of coins into dark and light by choosing one cutoff shade; Otsu's method finds the cutoff that keeps each pile as alike as possible.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers run it on the intensity histogram to get a threshold before binarizing an image. It assumes two dominant classes and unimodal-ish peaks, so it degrades on uneven lighting or when the foreground occupies very little area.
tiers.paperLevel: Choose threshold t minimizing intra-class intensity variance, equivalent to maximizing inter-class variance. It is a one-dimensional discrete analogue of Fisher's discriminant analysis, related to Jenks optimization, and equivalent to globally optimal k-means on the intensity histogram.

explainer.example: A scanned document with dark text on a light page: Otsu's method returns a mid-gray threshold, and pixels below it become text and above it become page.
